identification.summary: UNC5342 is Google Threat Intelligence Group's (GTIG) uncluster name for a North Korea (DPRK) threat actor that GTIG says it has tracked since February 2025 incorporating the EtherHiding technique into an ongoing social-engineering campaign [S1]. GTIG describes this as the first time it has observed a nation-state actor adopting EtherHiding [S1]. GTIG ties the campaign to what Palo Alto Networks dubbed Contagious Interview [S1]. GTIG describes the operation as ongoing, with a dual espionage and financial purpose [S1]. Operators pose as recruiters and lure software and web developers into running trojanized coding tests, which deliver the JADESNOW downloader and the INVISIBLEFERRET backdoor [S1].
identification.firstObserved: GTIG: tracked since February 2025 using EtherHiding in the campaign [S1]. The wider Contagious Interview campaign was first publicly reported by Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 in November 2023 [S9]. The UNC5342 cluster boundary versus the wider Contagious Interview activity is not defined in the sources gathered.
identification.notes: Name is a Google/Mandiant UNC designation; no Microsoft actor name is mapped in the source material gathered. GTIG says the campaign is the one Palo Alto Networks named Contagious Interview [S1]; Unit 42 tracked the cluster as CL-STA-0240 per press coverage [S6]. Cluster-boundary caution: Sysdig's EtherRAT finding (December 2025) was linked by Sysdig to Contagious Interview techniques but reporting says attribution is not settled, so EtherRAT is not treated here as confirmed UNC5342 tooling [S7]. Other vendor names for this activity (for example CrowdStrike Famous Chollima) were seen only in secondary summaries and are not asserted here. Do not merge with UNC5142, the separate financially motivated cluster behind CLEARFAKE that GTIG says originated EtherHiding use; GTIG does not describe UNC5142 as DPRK [S1].

attribution.sponsor: North Korea (DPRK), as assessed by GTIG [S1].
attribution.confidence: GTIG labels UNC5342 a North Korea (DPRK) threat actor and states the campaign has a dual purpose that aligns with North Korea's strategic goals, financial gain and espionage [S1]. The GTIG post does not give an explicit high/moderate/low confidence level for the DPRK attribution [S1]. No government attribution of UNC5342 specifically was found.
attribution.basis: GTIG technical analysis of the infection chain, smart-contract infrastructure and malware (JADESNOW, INVISIBLEFERRET) [S1]; alignment with the Contagious Interview campaign documented by Unit 42 [S1][S5][S6]. The detailed evidence behind the DPRK judgment is not itemised in the GTIG post [S1].

objectives: Financial gain (cryptocurrency theft) and espionage, which GTIG says align with North Korea's strategic goals [S1]. The malware steals browser data, credentials and cryptocurrency wallet data, and the campaign has been linked to numerous cryptocurrency heists [S1].

targeting.notes: GTIG says targets are software and web developers, particularly in cryptocurrency and technology sectors [S1]. Reporting on the related Silent Push findings says main targets are job applicants for cryptocurrency positions [S4]. Victim counts, names and geography are not given in the GTIG post [S1]. Targeting is of individuals, which can reach employers' systems and wallets through developer workstations (analyst note, not a sourced claim).

capabilities.summary: Social engineering: fake recruiters on LinkedIn and job boards move targets to Telegram or Discord, assign coding tests or project reviews requiring a GitHub download, and in some cases use ClickFix-style fake errors during video interviews [S1]. Fabricated companies named BlockNovas LLC, Angeloper Agency and SoftGlideLLC were used [S1]; Silent Push tied these to Contagious Interview [S4]. Initial loaders are often hosted on the npm registry [S1]. JADESNOW is a JavaScript downloader that fetches, decrypts and runs payloads from smart contracts on BNB Smart Chain and Ethereum, with data that may be Base64-encoded and XOR-encrypted [S1]. INVISIBLEFERRET is a backdoor that connects to C2 over port 3306, beacons host, user, OS and working directory, and supports command execution and file exfiltration [S1]. A credential-stealer component targets Chrome, Edge, MetaMask, Phantom and password managers such as 1Password, sending data to an attacker server and a private Telegram chat [S1]. BEAVERTAIL is listed as a second-stage JavaScript stealer for wallet, browser-extension and credential data [S1]. EtherHiding: payloads are held in smart-contract data or in transaction calldata, queried through block-explorer APIs (Binplorer, Blockchair, Blockcypher, Ethplorer), so the actor can update malware by changing the contract; the contract was updated more than 20 times in the first four months at about 1.37 USD gas per update [S1]. GTIG says use of multiple blockchains may indicate operational compartmentalization between North Korean teams [S1]. Windows, macOS and Linux are affected [S1].

campaigns.name: Contagious Interview first reported (Unit 42)
campaigns.summary: Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 first publicly reported fake-recruiter lures delivering BeaverTail (JavaScript stealer/loader in npm packages) and InvisibleFerret (Python backdoor); this is the campaign GTIG later ties UNC5342 to. UNC5342 itself was not named then.

campaigns.name: Fake video-conferencing apps
campaigns.summary: Press coverage of Unit 42 reporting says the campaign persisted after disclosure, using fake video-conferencing apps impersonating MiroTalk and FreeConference.com to deliver malware.

campaigns.name: EtherHiding adopted into Contagious Interview
campaigns.summary: GTIG says it has tracked UNC5342 incorporating EtherHiding into the ongoing social-engineering campaign since February 2025, with JADESNOW added to the chain.

campaigns.name: Front companies exposed
campaigns.summary: Silent Push, via press coverage, tied BlockNovas LLC, Angeloper Agency and SoftGlide LLC to Contagious Interview lures delivering BeaverTail, InvisibleFerret and OtterCookie.

campaigns.name: npm supply-chain link
campaigns.summary: GTIG states the UNC5342 smart contract was linked to a software supply-chain attack affecting React Native Aria and GlueStack through compromised npm packages in June 2025, citing Aikido. The Aikido report itself was not opened.

campaigns.name: GTIG publishes EtherHiding findings
campaigns.summary: GTIG publishes that UNC5342 is the first nation-state actor it has seen using EtherHiding, with infrastructure details on BNB Smart Chain and Ethereum.

campaigns.name: EtherRAT reported (attribution unsettled)
campaigns.summary: Sysdig reported EtherRAT, a Linux implant that resolves C2 through Ethereum smart contracts, on a Next.js server exploited via React2Shell (CVE-2025-55182) within two days of disclosure. Sysdig notes overlap with Contagious Interview (loader resembling BeaverTail) but hedges on whether DPRK actors or an imitator are responsible; one difference is that the sample downloads Node.js from nodejs.org. Not treated as UNC5342-confirmed.

diamond.adversary: DPRK-linked operators assessed by GTIG; GTIG suggests multiple blockchains may reflect compartmentalized teams [S1].
diamond.capability: Fake-recruiter social engineering, npm-hosted loaders, JADESNOW downloader, INVISIBLEFERRET backdoor, credential and wallet stealers, BEAVERTAIL [S1].
diamond.infrastructure: Smart contracts and transaction calldata on BNB Smart Chain and Ethereum (including burn-address transactions) as dead-drop resolvers, queried via public block-explorer APIs; C2 over port 3306; Telegram exfiltration; npm and GitHub hosting; fabricated recruiting companies [S1][S4].
diamond.victim: Software and web developers, especially in cryptocurrency and technology; crypto job applicants [S1][S4].
diamond.socioPolitical: Revenue generation and espionage aligned with DPRK strategic goals, per GTIG [S1].
diamond.technology: Developer workflows that run untrusted code (npm, GitHub, coding tests), public blockchains and free block-explorer APIs that cannot be taken down, and cross-platform Node.js and Python runtimes [S1].

gaps: GTIG does not state an explicit confidence level for DPRK attribution, and the evidence behind it is not itemised in the post [S1].

Relationship of UNC5342 to the whole Contagious Interview campaign (Unit 42 CL-STA-0240) and to other vendors' names (for example CrowdStrike Famous Chollima) is not confirmed from primary vendor documents; only secondary summaries were seen. Aliases were therefore not added.

The imported record associates EtherRAT with UNC5342; the sources gathered (Sysdig via press) do not confirm that, and attribution is described as unsettled [S7]. The Sysdig primary report was not opened.
No victim names, counts or loss figures tied to UNC5342 are public in the sources gathered [S1].
Aikido's report on the June 2025 npm compromise and Silent Push's original report were not opened; only press or GTIG citations were used [S1][S4].
Government attribution (DOJ, FBI, Treasury) of this specific cluster was not found.

Unit 42, Silent Push and Sysdig primary reports could not be fetched (thehackernews.com unreachable on re-check); secondary coverage and search snippets were used [S4][S5][S6][S7][S8]. GTIG post was fetched and read directly [S1].

Search summaries list other vendor names for Contagious Interview (CrowdStrike Famous Chollima, ESET DeceptiveDevelopment, Trend Micro Void Dokkaebi, Group-IB attribution to Lazarus, Recorded Future PurpleBravo) but no primary vendor document was opened, so none are added as aliases and cluster equivalence with UNC5342 is unverified.
Sysdig's EtherRAT report: whether actors differ from UNC5342 and whether GTIG shares the DPRK link is unresolved [S7][S8].

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Key terrain is the developer workstation and the software supply chain (npm, GitHub, coding-assessment repositories) plus the crypto wallets and browser credential stores on those hosts; the blockchain itself is adversary infrastructure that cannot be taken down [S1]. STEP 2: Environment effects: recruiting platforms (LinkedIn, job boards), Telegram and Discord are the contact channels, and public block explorers are the payload delivery path, so network blocking has limited effect on the dead-drop [S1]. STEP 3: Adversary model: DPRK teams run fake-recruiter lures, deliver JADESNOW then INVISIBLEFERRET and credential stealers, and exfiltrate over port 3306 and Telegram [S1]. STEP 4: MLCOA: continued targeting of crypto and tech developers for wallet and credential theft to generate revenue [S1]. MDCOA (analyst judgment): the same lure aimed at cleared or defense-contractor developers, or use of compromised npm packages to reach many organizations, converting financial tradecraft into espionage; GTIG states the campaign has an espionage purpose [S1]. Candidate indicators: unsolicited recruiter contact moving to Telegram or Discord, coding tests requiring GitHub or npm installs, Node.js processes querying block-explorer APIs, outbound traffic on port 3306 to non-database hosts, and portable Python interpreters installed by scripts [S1].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: share the Contagious Interview lure pattern with the force, especially personnel on professional networking sites, and track block-explorer API lookups from workstations as a detection source [S1]. (2) Authorities: actions against the actor's infrastructure are limited because payloads sit on public blockchains; GTIG notes some API providers acted but others stayed unresponsive, so takedown requests rest with providers and law enforcement rather than military authorities [S1]. (3) Mission assurance: restrict running of untrusted code on mission and administrative systems, and control npm and GitHub access for developers [S1]. (4) Coordination: coordinate with DC3, the DIB cybersecurity program and Cyber Command partners for contractor developers; use GTIG, Unit 42 and Silent Push reporting for indicator sharing [S1][S4][S5].
